newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian dollar recovers after RBA hiccup.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian dollar recovers after RBA hiccup.

text.p: The Australian dollar recovered from a brief dip on the release of the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) bulletin to finish the day comfortably within its month-long range and slightly up on its open.

The RBA did not rule out a rate cut in its October Bulletin, but expressed concerns over the pace of wages growth threatening low inflation, and the realisation that a cut was not a formality saw the dollar recover its initial dip, traders said.
By 5.00 p.m. (0700 GMT), it was at US$0.7910/15, having dipped to under US$0.7890 on the bulletin's release, compared with an early US$0.7896/01 and US$0.7925/30 late Monday.

"Basically the market got very, very bearish, goes down to US$0.7887 given, got very short then realised that they are talking about a rate cut, but they want to see more on wages growth and inflation which could take a while," one trader said.
"It could be another couple of months before we actually see a rate cut, so you don't get short on a day when everyone knows you're going to get one anyhow,' he said.

In the quarterly review of the economy and its prospects in the October Bulletin, the RBA said that other things being equal a reduction in inflationary expectations would support the case for a rate cut, as would the economy being weaker than expected.

"On the other hand, on current growth projections, and without evidence that wages are adjusting to the lower inflation environment, a relaxation of monetary policy could have the effect of storing up problems for the future," the RBA said.

New enterprise bargaining agreements were not yet reflecting the economy-wide moderation in wages growth, "raising concerns that wages growth might accelerate when labour market conditions begin to tighten," the RBA said.
Economists said the tough talk on wages and the threat they were to maintaining low inflation made it less certain that rates would be cut in November, as had been widely expected.

Bonds and bills weakened on the bulletin, most noticeably at the short end. March bill futures, which had traded on Tuesday at an implied yield 68 points under the 7.0 percent official cash rate, closed Wednesday 45 points under cash.

"They want to see further evidence of lower labour costs before they are willing to reduce official interest rates further, so it's certainly not a lay-down misere (sure bet) for a rate cut in November," Colonial State Bank senior economist Craig James said.

Ahead of the release of the RBA bulletin, data released by Westpac Bank showed October consumer sentiment fell to its lowest level in a year, which Westpac said strengthened the case for a November rate cut.

The focus is now in third quarter wages data due next week. Economists surveyed by Reuters expect wages growth to come in at 3.7 percent in annual terms, a figure that they said, before the bulletin was released, would leave room for a rate cut.
The RBA Board next meets on November 5, and most expectations had centred on a cut being announced the following day, but the RBA can change rates on any day it chooses.
Despite the dollar being held to a US$0.7855/7965 range over the past month, there was good two way trade, dealers said.
"There is also a rumour there is a very big bid in the market at US$0.7885, it's been floating around for the best part of the day," the trader said.

On the crosses, the Australian dollar finished a touch higher at 88.76/86 yen from an early 88.60/70 and 88.71/81 late on Tuesday. In trade weighted terms it closed at 58.6, level with its previous close and up slightly on its opening 58.5.
